note: The Sages remembered that Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai would take a myrtle branch and dance in front of a bride, calling out 'A fair and attractive bride.' Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak went further and danced juggling three myrtle branches. Rabbi Zeira objected that the old man was making the scholars look foolish. But when Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, an honor said to be given to only one or two people in a generation.
why: The Gemara is collecting the songs and praises the Sages offered at weddings and ordinations. This account of dancing before brides belongs to that set, and right afterward Rabbi Zeira concedes that the old man's branch is what earned him his reward.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the destruction of the Second Temple, remembered here for dancing at weddings.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak
people.about: An elderly Sage, called 'the old man' here, who juggled myrtle branches as he danced before brides.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Babylonian-born Sage who moved to the Land of Israel; at first he disapproved of the juggling.

terms.meaning: A fragrant evergreen shrub; its branches were carried at weddings and celebrations.
A sign of divine honor, recalling the pillar of fire that led Israel in the wilderness. Here it marks someone as one of the greatest people of his generation.
A religious commandment or good deed. Bringing joy to a bride and groom is counted as one.

note: A man known as bar Shatya suffered from bouts of insanity, and he sold some of his property. Two witnesses came and said he had sold it while insane, which would cancel the sale; two others said he had sold it while sane. Rav Ashi ruled that the two pairs cancel each other out, so the property stays with bar Shatya. The Gemara adds that this applies only to land he inherited from his fathers; property he had bought himself goes to the buyer, since he may have bought it while insane too.
why: The Gemara is asking what happens when witnesses who signed a document are contradicted by others when they are not present. Rav Nahman says to set two against two and leave money with its owner, and cites bar Shatya's sale as his precedent.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, who cites this case to support his ruling.

people.name: bar Shatya
people.about: A man with periodic bouts of insanity; his name means roughly 'son of a madman'.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, remembered as a chief editor of the Talmud, who ruled on the sale.

terms.meaning: When two witnesses say one thing and two say the opposite, neither pair is believed over the other, so the court acts as if no testimony was given.
Property inherited from one's family. The court presumes it still belongs to the heir unless someone proves otherwise.

note: Rav Yehuda tells, and an early teaching confirms, how the marriage contract took its form. At first a groom pledged two hundred dinars to a virgin bride and one hundred to a widow, to be set aside in cash, and men grew old without marrying. The Sages had the money kept in the bride's father's house, but an angry husband could easily say 'Go to your marriage contract.' Then they had it kept in the husband's house, where rich women made it into silver and gold baskets and poor women into a chamber pot, and husbands still said 'Take your marriage contract and leave.' Finally Shimon ben Shatah ruled that the husband writes that all his property guarantees the contract.
why: The discussion has been about whether a husband may sell property while it is pledged for his wife's marriage contract; this history explains where that lien on all his property came from.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, student of Rav and Shmuel, who reports this history.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: A leader of the Sages in the first century BCE, credited with the final form of the marriage contract.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document in which a husband promises his wife a sum of money if he divorces her or dies. It protects her and makes divorce costly.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
A silver coin; two hundred dinars was a large sum.
